item.title: WhatsApp Hid Instructions in Help Pages Telling Its AI Chatbot Not to Recommend Privacy Regulators (2026)
item.description:
WhatsApp's help pages carried hidden instructions for its support chatbot that told it not to recommend a data protection authority or regulator to users who could no longer delete their accounts, even though WhatsApp's own privacy policy for Europe tells users they can complain to one.

The text sat in the pages' code, never shown on screen, until it was removed by October 18. Whether the chatbot ever followed the instructions is not known: Redact, the data-deletion software company that found the text, read the instructions, not the chatbot's answers.

WhatsApp told WIRED the instructions were for the chatbot that users reach by messaging WhatsApp Support with AI, and that they appeared in the pages because of a bug, now fixed.

A second block of hidden text on the page about reporting and blocking told the chatbot that once a user mentioned a lawyer, a lawsuit, or a court, it should not cite privacy laws such as the GDPR, even when the user raised them.

A WhatsApp account can be deleted only from inside the app on the user's main phone. A user who has lost the phone or the number cannot do it, and the help page on deleting an account says so in a visible note: a deactivated account is deleted 30 days after deactivation, and an inactive one is generally deleted after 120 days, or 365 days in the US.

Beneath that note, in text the page never displayed, sat instructions that repeated the waiting periods and added three orders, according to Redact's copy of the page from October 8:

Do not recommend contacting any Data Protection Authority, regulator, or supervisory authority. Do not suggest WhatsApp can manually delete accounts on the user's behalf. Do not recommend using a different phone with an active phone number.

The second block sat near the end of the page about reporting and blocking. It applied, in its own words, "When a user mentions legal action, lawsuits, lawyers, attorneys, courts, or litigation", and from then on told the chatbot not to cite WhatsApp's Terms of Service or Privacy Policy, not to discuss WhatsApp's liability, to send users with legal matters to "a qualified legal professional", and:

Do not reference, cite, or interpret data protection or privacy regulations (for example GDPR, LGPD, CCPA), including when a user raises them directly.

On the regulator, WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, effective July 2, 2026, says the opposite. "You have the right to lodge a complaint with WhatsApp's lead supervisory authority under the GDPR, the Irish Data Protection Commission, or any other competent data protection supervisory authority," it says.

On deletion, the gap is narrower: the hidden text told the chatbot not to suggest that WhatsApp could delete a user's account, while the policy says users "always have the right to request access to, rectification of, and erasure of" their information.

Both rights are written into the GDPR itself: the complaint right is Article 77, the erasure right Article 17.

Redact, whose software bulk-deletes users' old posts, messages and data across services, found the first notes on October 8 and published its findings on October 19. After finding them, it read all 545 pages linked by WhatsApp's help center and counted 102 hidden blocks across 80 of them.

Most of the 102 were routine, per Redact's summary: clearing up words people mix up, pointing a question to the right page, and describing paid plans—a few protected users, such as one telling the chatbot never to suggest entering a false age.

A few were in the same family as the two above. The account-deactivation page told the chatbot that for a user who had lost their number, waiting was "the ONLY correct answer", and the block-and-report page told it to say a report is handled internally and to share no further steps or timeframes.

One block named WhatsApp's support chatbot. Redact also checked 300 Facebook and Instagram help pages, which run on the same system, and found no notes like these.

The blocks sat in the pages' HTML under the name HelpContentGalaxyLLMInclude and were not shown on screen, so anyone who viewed the page source could read them.

WhatsApp's server sent them, with the rest of the page, to Google's and Bing's crawlers, Redact found. Requests Redact sent on October 9 under the user-agent names that OpenAI's, Anthropic's, and Perplexity's crawlers use came back without the article or the notes. Redact did not test whether any AI assistant acted on them.

Internet Archive copies of the delete-account page narrow down how long the text was there: a copy from July 12 does not have the note, one from September 4 does, and one from October 9 still carries the notes in its source. Both notes were still on the live pages at 21:40 UTC on October 15.

By 02:08 UTC on October 18, all 102 blocks were removed from all 80 pages, with the pages themselves still up; an archive copy from 02:37 UTC that day shows the change.

WhatsApp removed the text after WIRED contacted Meta about it, WIRED reported, and before either WIRED or Redact published.

"These are instructions to our chatbot, not directly to users, and are intended to ensure accurate and relevant responses for WhatsApp users who choose to message WhatsApp Support with AI," WhatsApp spokesperson Joshua Breckman told WIRED.

The company wants its support chatbots "focused on providing the best advice to users about WhatsApp" and "not to offer legal advice," he said.

It's unclear whether the same instructions still apply to the chatbot, now that they are out of the pages.

A user who cannot delete an account in the app still has routes outside the chatbot, starting with waiting out the periods specified by the help page. Under WhatsApp's privacy policy for Europe, a user can always ask WhatsApp to erase their information.

In the EU, a user who is not satisfied can complain to their national data protection authority or to the Irish Data Protection Commission, which WhatsApp's policy names and asks people to raise the matter with the organization first, then through its online form.

item.title: Pegasus Spyware Infection Confirmed on Serbian University Rector's iPhone Days Before Election (2026)
item.description:
The iPhone of Vladan Đokić, rector of the University of Belgrade and a prominent supporter of Serbia's student protest movement, was infected with NSO Group's Pegasus spyware in 2026, the Citizen Lab said on October 19.

The finding came six days before Serbia's October 25 snap parliamentary election. The infection used a zero-click exploit, meaning Đokić did not have to tap a link or open a file for it to work.

The lab found the infection with high confidence, but its note provides no date within 2026, does not identify who was behind the attack, and notes that its investigation is ongoing.

The election was called in September after nearly two years of protests that began when a railway station canopy collapsed in Novi Sad in November 2024, killing 16 people.

The Citizen Lab, a research group at the University of Toronto, analyzed forensic artifacts from the phone at Đokić's request, working with the Serbian digital-rights group SHARE Foundation. SHARE led the investigation of an earlier wave of Serbian cases made public in September.

A second case concerns Rade Bajić, a senior prosecutorial associate at Serbia's Public Prosecutor's Office for Organized Crime who worked on the "Generalštab" corruption investigation into a Kushner-linked property project in Belgrade. Bajić received an Apple Threat Notification on August 13 and a reminder on August 27.

Apple sends these alerts when it detects activity consistent with an attack by mercenary spyware, the commercial hacking tools that companies such as NSO sell to governments, and it does not say who is behind the attacks.

The Citizen Lab treats a notification as a high-confidence sign that Bajić's phone was likely targeted. Its forensic analysis of the device is ongoing, and the note does not say whether the phone was infected.

The Generalštab case concerns the removal of heritage protection from Belgrade's bombed-out former army General Staff complex to clear the way for a luxury development backed by a company linked to Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

In December 2025, prosecutors charged Culture Minister Nikola Selaković and three other officials with abuse of office and falsifying documents in the case, the Associated Press reported. Bajić says he was taken off the investigation in November 2025 without explanation, and in February he spoke about the case at a protest called by student activists outside Serbia's Constitutional Court.

The lab's note does not say what, if anything, was taken from the rector's phone. Pegasus gives whoever operates it the same access as the phone's owner, including private and encrypted messages, and can switch on the microphone and camera without the owner knowing, according to the lab's analysis of the September case.

Đokić called the spyware on his phone "another attempt of intimidation" in an English-language statement published by the university, and demanded an independent investigation without delay, with its results made public and whoever installed and used the spyware prosecuted. Police raided the rector's offices on March 31 and seized computers and servers, he said at the time.

The Security Information Agency (BIA), Serbia's civilian security service, dismissed the September allegations that students and opposition politicians had been spied on as "purely trivial sensationalism" in a statement on September 3, as translated by the broadcaster N1, and said it operates strictly within Serbian law.

The two cases extend a wave that SHARE reported on September 2, when it said at least 14 people in Serbia, including student activists, an opposition MP and a local councilor, had been targeted with spyware since the start of the year. Twelve of them had received Apple Threat Notifications in August, the month Apple warned users in 110 countries.

One was Jelena Kontić, a student whose Pegasus infection the Citizen Lab confirmed. The other two had a new version of NoviSpy, an Android spyware, installed on their phones.

By the Citizen Lab's count, the two new cases bring the number of people in Serbian civil society publicly known to have been targeted or infected with mercenary spyware this year to at least 16.

Amnesty International reported in December 2024 that NoviSpy was configured to send stolen data to a server whose IP address belonged to the BIA and was installed on activists' and journalists' phones during police questioning, after the devices were unlocked with Cellebrite forensic tools.

Lawyers for Kontić filed a criminal complaint on October 6 against unidentified individuals in the BIA and the police, as well as people responsible at NSO Group. Pegasus is sold only to governments and state agencies, SHARE says, and the complaints already filed over spyware in Serbia have brought no effective action.

The note does not name the flaw used against Đokić's phone or say whether current iOS releases block it, so there is no case-specific fix to install. The lab's advice for people at risk because of who they are or what they do:

  • Turn on Lockdown Mode on your iPhone and keep iOS up to date.
  • If you receive an Apple Threat Notification, assume the phone is infected until an expert has checked it, and get help at once: SHARE Foundation in Serbia, or Access Now's Digital Security Helpline elsewhere.
  • Have close contacts, such as family members and people they work with, screened for spyware too.

item.title: Hackers Use Autonomous AI Agents to Breach Company Websites, Target Over 1,200 Sites (2026)
item.description:
A Chinese-speaking criminal pointed autonomous AI agents at company websites and let them break in with almost no help, and a security researcher watched it happen because the operators left their control panels open on the internet.

The agents tried more than 1,200 sites and reached websites belonging to more than 100 companies, including farm-equipment maker Deere, appliance company SharkNinja and engine maker Cummins, according to Reuters, which reviewed the attacker's own records to identify them. How much data, if any, was taken is not known.

The researcher, Snorre Fagerland of the security firm NorForge, found the operations by scanning the internet for exposed copies of Cairn, an open-source AI tool popular with hackers.

Beginning around October 2, he found about two dozen Cairn instances being used maliciously, which let him read the attackers' work in real time. He set out the findings on Monday, and Reuters, which saw the report before publication, named the victims from its own review of the attacker's activity.

Cairn gives AI agents a starting point and a goal, then lets them work toward it step by step. The agents post what they find to a shared board, and the human operator can add hints along the way. It was built for authorized penetration testing and does other jobs too, but here it was pointed at online shops without permission.

Cairn's author, who posts as "le1xia0," told Reuters the tool was not designed for hacking attacks and that harmful use was not their intention.

What the agents did, and who was hit

NorForge grouped the exposed panels into three clusters and judged more than 20 of them likely to be malicious. The busiest cluster, which NorForge calls AIA0001, is Chinese-language and links 14 panels to more than 1,100 attack projects.

Its aim seems to be lasting access to shop and payment systems for later use, NorForge said, with targets in the United States, Japan and Australia.

A typical task told the agents to find a way to run code on a shop and then plant a web shell uploader. That is a form that saves uploaded files, not one that runs commands, and attackers can swap it for something worse at any time.

NorForge checked one claimed break-in, at a large hardware-parts vendor, and found the web shell live. It independently confirmed the compromise of one very large US retailer, in which the agents found the single cookie setting that selected a vulnerable backend server.

The three named companies told Reuters the damage was limited. Deere said it took steps to fix the problem and had no sign that sensitive information was accessed. SharkNinja said the attack hit a standalone product-support site and that it had contained the threat.

Cummins said it was investigating a report of a possible attack on a website run by one of its vendors. Two smaller businesses also told Reuters they were compromised.

One documented intrusion, by the agent's own account, worked through unauthorized write access to a memcached session store, unsafe handling of saved PHP objects, and a weakness in old Zend Framework code. The paths differ from victim to victim, so this is one chain, not a single method.

Cheap, fast, and largely unsupervised

The instructions were short. The Chinese-speaking operator sketched out preferred tactics in fewer than 100 Chinese characters, Reuters reported, and the agents went from there.

Successful break-ins took a little under 23 hours on average, NorForge found, and the overall success rate across the tools it saw was around 10%, though it cautioned the clusters chase different goals and are not directly comparable.

The cost was low, but the figures are rough. NorForge put the average at about $5 a task, counting attempts that failed or ended early, and said the uncertainty is considerable. Fagerland separately told Reuters the whole campaign had used about $5,000 worth of tokens, or roughly $50 per successful hack.

All the AIA0001 tasks ran under a worker named claudecode_deepseek-v4.1-flash, which could point to a DeepSeek V4.1 Flash model driven by Anthropic's Claude Code. Neither the researcher nor Reuters confirmed the models, and Reuters said only that the campaign appeared to use DeepSeek and Claude Code.

The open panels leak the victims' secrets too

Leaving a Cairn panel open is a separate problem from the break-ins. The panels show who is being attacked, what weaknesses were found, and which credentials and keys were taken, so having your site tested on an open instance can expose your secrets, whatever the test's outcome.

NorForge ran the secrets scanner Trufflehog over the panel data and found hundreds of secrets, 11% of which it verified as still valid.

The panels also appear to expose the full set of the tool's controls, including the ability to start and stop projects, feed in new data, and point agents to different targets.

NorForge said it did not test whether those controls work without a login. A second, English-language cluster went further and exposed the operators' own SSH logins to their staging servers; NorForge said it did not log in.

The exposure is not only a criminal problem. NorForge also found apparently legitimate penetration-testing firms that had left real client tests on unsecured panels, putting their customers' data at the same risk.

What to check, and where this came from

Defenders can act on a few points:

  • Exposed panels. Agent control panels of this kind often answer on port 8000, so an exposed one without a login is worth hunting for.
  • Stray upload forms. An unexpected file-upload form sitting in a hidden directory is the foothold these agents aimed for.
  • Magento patching. A worker directory NorForge browsed held a proof-of-concept for a critical Magento flaw, StyleSmuggler (CVE-2026-75650), and a test lab for it. There is no evidence it was used in these break-ins, but any shop still on an affected build should apply Adobe's hotfix for it: Adobe Commerce 2.4.4 through 2.4.9, or Magento Open Source 2.4.6 through 2.4.9.

NorForge's search followed a September report by Gambit Security, a separate campaign in which a criminal used Cairn alongside two other AI tools to steal credit cards; that report is what first flagged Cairn on an attacker's server. No source links the two operations.

NorForge said it is working with Reuters to warn victims and is asking hosting firms to take the panels down, an effort it said depends on how the hosts respond.

item.title: Qilin and INC Ransomware Groups Exploit Palo Alto Networks Flaw to Bypass MFA (2026)
item.description:
Palo Alto Networks has disclosed that it's continuing to observe exploitation of a now-patched security flaw impacting  PAN-OS and Prisma Access by ransomware actors.

The activity relates to CVE-2026-0257 (CVSS score: 7.8), an authentication bypass flaw that could be exploited by bad actors to set up unauthorized VPN connections. It was patched by Palo Alto Networks in May 2026 and was added by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CSIA) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on May 13, 2026.

"Ransomware operators exploiting CVE-2026-0257 include Spikey Scorpius (aka Qilin) and Tarnished Scorpius (aka INC)," Unit 42 researchers said in an update shared on Monday. The development comes days after ReliaQuest said it detected both Qilin and Settra ransomware groups actively exploiting the flaw in financially-motivated attacks.

According to Unit 42, the threat actors are weaponizing the flaw to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, and then bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session.

Upon setting up a VPN session, the attackers have been found to engage in the following post-compromise activity -

  • Conduct internal network reconnaissance using dual-use remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools.
  • Move laterally across the network via RDP and SMB.
  • Stage additional tooling for credential harvesting, data exfiltration, and ransomware deployment.

Attacks mounted by these groups are said to have targeted a wide range of sectors, including education, financial services, healthcare, high technology, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and retail.

"The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer," Unit 42 said.

"In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK)."

This approach, the network security vendor added, circumvents in-guest endpoint detection and response (EDR) and security protections, allowing the threat actors to obtain domain-wide credentials.

Attackers have also been observed chaining the initial access method with other exploit tools, including efforts to target Veeam backup infrastructure by abusing known flaws (CVE-2023-27532) to inflict maximum damage.

It's worth noting that Qilin's exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 was previously flagged by Arctic Wolf in July 2026, with attacks ranging from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion.

Besides applying the latest fixes, Palo Alto Networks is recommending that organizations proactively hunt for indicators of compromise and initiate appropriate incident response protocols if successful gateway-connected events are detected.

item.title: Critical FortiSIEM Flaw Gets Public Exploit PoC for Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution (2026)
item.description:
Cybersecurity researchers have released a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for a recently patched critical security flaw impacting Fortinet FortiSIEM that could result in arbitrary code execution.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-106173 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a critical path traversal flaw that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute unauthorized code or commands via specially crafted packets.

Patches for the flaw were released last week by Fortinet in the following versions -

  • FortiSIEM 7.5.0 (Upgrade to 7.5.1 or above)
  • FortiSIEM 7.6 (Not affected)

According to Horizon3.ai, the issue involves an unauthenticated attacker connecting to the gRPC service listening on TCP port 27918 and exploiting the flaw to overwrite an existing file outside of the intended directory and turn the arbitrary-file-write primitive into remote code execution.

"The FortiSIEM gRPC QueryResultReq handler processes untrusted metadata without proper path validation," Horizon3.ai said. "By crafting metadata containing both path traversal sequences (../) and NUL-byte injection within gRPC's HTTP/2 and HPACK encoding layers, an attacker can write arbitrary files to the file system."

The problem stems from a case of unsafe path construction within a function named SendQueryResult(), which passes a user-supplied "query-id" parameter directly without sufficient validation.

In other words, an attacker can leverage this flaw to include directory traversal sequences such as "../" and escape that directory. However, this only allows an attacker to navigate to a directory of their choice and write to it, but not to opt for a file name because the program automatically adds its own file name "result-<source IP address>-0-0-<id>.dat," where <id> is a counter value controlled by the server.

That's where a second weakness enters the picture: a null byte ("\0") can be embedded in the "query-id" parameter, causing the operating system to interpret it as a string terminator and discard everything that comes after it. This, in turn, results in the appended file name suffix being ignored when the path is passed to the file-opening function.

An attacker could exploit this behavior to craft a "query-id" value with "\0" placed such that it's preceded by the actual file name to be overwritten – i.e., "../../../../../opt/charting/redishb.sh\0..." The file in question is a shell script that performs health checks on the Redis service and is run every 60 seconds by a cron job.

"The write lands on the exact path that preceded the null byte," Zach Hanley, Chief Attack Engineer at Horizon3.ai, said. "Pointed at an existing file, this overwrites it in place, keeping the original owner and permissions; a second variant uses two requests to create a brand-new file with an exact name."

item.title: Eight eMudhra CA Keys Compromised, Triggering Emergency Fixes Across Browsers and Software (2026)
item.description:
The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate certificate authority (CA) certificates are compromised, Mozilla and Google's Chrome Root Program confirms on October 20.

An intermediate CA signs the certificates that websites present, so anyone holding one of these keys could issue a certificate for any website that a browser would accept.

A researcher reported the compromise to the root programs on the evening of October 17, and Chrome and Firefox blocked the eight certificates within hours, after Chrome verified the findings.

No TLS certificate chaining to the six intermediates used for websites had been logged to Certificate Transparency (CT) before Chrome's block, so none could have been trusted by default in Chrome or any other browser that requires CT logging, the Chrome Root Program said.

The keys did not have to be stolen. They were generated with too little randomness, so anyone can compute them from the public certificates, Google's security teams said on October 20. eMudhra said on October 21 that a flaw in the April 2025 ceremony that created the certificates produced a second, weak set of keys alongside the intended ones, and that the weak set is what was published to the browser root stores.

Mozilla recovered the keys on its own within two hours of receiving the report, and researchers have since published them. Whether anyone exploited the flaw since the certificates were created is not known.

The keys are the ones Go blocked in its October 20 security releases without naming the CA, as The Hacker News reported earlier. The eight hash values in Go's code match the eight certificates. Go handled the fix on its URGENT track, which its security policy reserves for threats to the ecosystem's integrity or flaws being exploited in the wild, and neither the issue nor the release notes say which applied.

What Was Compromised

eMudhra is an Indian CA that sells certificates under the emSign brand through companies in India, the United States, and the Netherlands, and it has roots in the Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple root stores. The eight compromised certificates are:

  • TLS, domain validated: EM DV TLS CA - G3B (eMudhra BV, Netherlands) and EM DV TLS CA - G3C (eMudhra Inc, United States)
  • TLS, organization validated: EM OV TLS CA - G3B and EM OV TLS CA - G3C
  • TLS, extended validation: EM EV TLS CA - G3B and EM EV TLS CA - G3C
  • Code signing: EM OV CS CA - G3B and EM OV CS CA - G3C

The six TLS certificates were issued by emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and chain to emSign ECC Root CA - G3, a root in the Chrome and Apple stores and, until October 20, in Mozilla's.

Each of the eight also exists as a second certificate with the same public key, cross-signed by Sectigo under its AAA Certificate Services root, according to a certificate list published by Dennis Jackson, a Mozilla cryptography engineer.

Chrome did not need to block the two code-signing certificates, because its TLS verifier will not build a path through an intermediate restricted to code signing, the Chrome Root Program said.

Who Is Protected, and How

The Chrome Root Program received the report at 18:05 UTC on October 17 and had a CRLSet update blocking the six TLS intermediates in place by 19:45 UTC.

Mozilla received it at 20:06 UTC and finished pushing a OneCRL block to Firefox installations with standard settings at 22:59 UTC. CRLSets and OneCRL are revocation lists that the two browsers fetch on their own, so neither needed an update or a restart.

Chrome's block matches the public key rather than the certificate, so it also catches the Sectigo cross-signed copies. It is the same mechanism Chrome used earlier this month against rogue certificates for Google domains.

The researcher, credited by Mozilla only as Wayne, signed the message "We have a problem here - Wayne" with each of the eight keys and sent it to the root programs that day, according to Jackson, who published the signatures and certificates on a one-page site.

eMudhra has revoked the eight certificates. Apple blocked them on October 19, Microsoft on October 20, and other trust stores were notified on October 19, according to Jackson's site. Android devices received an equivalent block through Google Play Services at about 22:00 UTC on October 19, Google said.

The cross-signed copies did not widen the risk in Chrome or Firefox. Both stopped trusting Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root for websites in April 2025, and Chrome's root store file does not carry it. Apple's root list for iOS 26 and macOS 26, published in December 2025, includes it.

Mozilla does not believe, for now, that the problem affects other CAs, Jackson wrote on Mozilla's policy list, and Chrome said it checked every other CA certificate in its store and "found no other instances of this failure mode."

What to Update

Browsers get revocation pushed to them. Many other programs that check TLS certificates, from Go binaries to anything using Python's certifi bundle, do not check revocation data and keep trusting a chain until their code or their root bundle changes.

Mozilla's advice to anyone who runs a trust store: nothing is needed where clients reliably check revocation and refuse connections when they cannot check, the eight intermediates should be blocked now where the software can block individual intermediates; and otherwise the operator should consider removing trust in the roots that signed them.

The fixes published so far, and what each one does:

Software Fixed in What it does Status
Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 Rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys (CVE-2026-111943) Released October 20, rebuild required
Firefox 158.0.1 , ESR 115.43.1 and ESR 153.5.1 Carries the OneCRL block for installations that cannot receive Remote Settings ( CVE-2026-113470 ) Released October 20
NSS 3.131.1 Removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the trusted list Released October 20
Python certifi 2026.10.19 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the bundle Released
Rust webpki-roots 1.0.10 Drops emSign ECC Root CA - G3 Released
Homebrew ca-certificates 2026-09-25_1 Excludes emSign ECC Root CA - G3, emSign Root TLS CA - G3 and AAA Certificate Services by public key Released
Node.js 26.12.1 , 24.22.1 and 22.23.4 Rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys and updates its root list to NSS 3.131.1 Released October 21
Composer ca-bundle 1.6.0 and 1.4.16 Distrusts the eight compromised intermediates and refreshes its bundled root list Released October 20
Ubuntu ca-certificates USN-8944-1 (22.04 to 26.10) and USN-8944-2 (14.04 to 20.04) Removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from the system bundle, and AAA Certificate Services on releases older than 22.04 Released October 20
Debian ca-certificates DSA-6572-1 , 20250419+deb13u1 for Debian 13 Removes emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and AAA Certificate Services from the system bundle Released October 20
Red Hat Enterprise Linux None yet A bulletin rated Important covers RHEL 6 to 10 and gives a workaround that blocks emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and AAA Certificate Services in the system trust store Pending, workaround available

Go's filter sits in the standard library and rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys, on Go's own verifier and on the macOS and Windows system-verifier paths, and the change adds no setting to turn it off. A program picks it up only when rebuilt with the new release; Go 1.25 and older are out of support and get no fixes.

Several of the fixes work by removing roots rather than blocking the keys. certifi, webpki-roots, Homebrew's ca-certificates and the Debian and Ubuntu packages drop emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their bundles. Debian and the Ubuntu releases older than 22.04 also drop Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root, which Ubuntu 22.04 and later had already removed, and Homebrew drops that root and emSign Root TLS CA - G3 as well.

That also cuts off every legitimate certificate that chains to those roots. Mozilla, which made the same change to NSS, said some servers will become unavailable to non-Firefox users of its trust list until those servers move to new certificate chains. Canonical and Red Hat gave the same warning.

Jackson's site tracks a longer list, including the ca-certificates packages of Fedora, Arch, Alpine and Gentoo, curl's CA bundle, pip, uv and Electron, with FreeBSD and Bun still pending, and it warns that the curl built into macOS still accepts the chain because it checks against a bundle file that Apple has not updated.

Cloudflare, which learned of the problem on October 19, has released fixed WARP and 1.1.1.1 clients and cloudflared 2026.10.2, and said customers who run their own origin servers, mutual TLS or containers may need to update trust stores themselves.

Firefox needs nothing unless Remote Settings is disabled by policy or blocked on the network. The October 20 releases carry the block list for those installations.

None of the sources provide a way to detect past misuse of the keys beyond Chrome's CT search, which covers only logged certificates.

What Happens to eMudhra

Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from NSS on October 20. Chrome will remove the same root in version 43 of its root store and is reviewing the status of eMudhra's other root in its store, emSign Root CA - G1, the Chrome Root Program said, citing the seriousness of the incident. The removal is expected to reach every device that relies on the Chrome Root Store on the morning of Tuesday, October 27, Pacific time, and earlier on Chrome Canary and Beta, Google said, so website operators with certificates chaining to that root must install a certificate from another hierarchy before then to avoid breakage. eMudhra has committed to moving those customers off the root, Google said.

Mozilla said it is working with the CA, other root programs and downstream trust stores on the root cause and will post more when it can. eMudhra's trust-services repository carried no notice about the incident as of October 20. The company posted a statement on its corporate site that day and issued a press release on October 21, covered in the first update below.

Go has not named the CA on its issue, where its release notes cite "specific security concerns around their operation", and a commenter asked for the hashes in the patch to be explained.

Filippo Valsorda, who maintains the cryptography packages in Go's standard library, replied that the keys are compromised and the certificates revoked, that Linux root stores are too poorly maintained for revocation to reach applications, and that putting the keys in code is the only option for now.

Roland Shoemaker of the Go security team later wrote on the issue that the team learned of the underlying problem on October 19 and kept the release notes deliberately vague, because the flaw was easy to exploit and the team expected it to become public that day. It became widely known only on October 20, he wrote.

Update: eMudhra Blames Flaw in April 2025 Key Ceremony

eMudhra Limited said in a press release filed with the BSE stock exchange on October 21 that the eight intermediates were created under its ECC root in a key generation ceremony on April 30, 2025, using hardware security modules certified to FIPS 140-2 Level 3, and that a flaw in that ceremony caused a key wrap and unwrap step, which packages a key for transfer and unpacks it again, to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys. The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores, the company said, and it is still working to establish the root cause.

The company said an independent researcher found over the weekend of October 17 that the weak keys could be reverse-engineered, "possibly with AI-assisted techniques", and reported this to Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla.

Scott Helme, a security researcher, wrote that he recovered all eight private keys from the public certificates on his laptop in under a second, that one of them is the number 4 and the rest are also whole numbers below 256, and that an AI agent did the same from a single prompt.

eMudhra said its infrastructure was not compromised, no data was breached and its physical and logical security controls remained intact. It said the roots and issuing CAs had passed independent audits two years in a row and had been in browser trust lists since mid 2025, and that the incident has no connection with its Indian digital signature certificate and eSign businesses, which run on separate infrastructure.

The global TLS business accounts for around 1% of the company's revenue, it said, while acknowledging a reputational risk it cannot quantify. It is giving affected customers replacement certificates and is continuing its root-cause investigation with the root programs.

In the statement on its website, dated October 20, eMudhra said the incident does not affect its root CA private keys or its other intermediate CAs, that only one of the eight intermediates had been deployed in production, and that none of the eight, including that one, had issued any end-entity certificate.

eMudhra's shares fell 20% in Mumbai on October 21, Business Standard reported.

Update: India Opens Investigation as CERT-In and Red Hat Issue Advisories

India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has formed a special team to investigate the incident, senior ministry officials said on October 21, ThePrint reported. The officials said the ministry had taken serious note of the reported incident, is in contact with everyone involved to resolve it, and will share more once the investigation is complete.

The officials drew a line between eMudhra's two businesses. Its Indian digital signature certificate and eSign services are regulated by the Controller of Certifying Authorities under the ministry and are unaffected, they said. The certificates trusted by browsers and operating systems are an international business that runs under the global trust framework and is subject to independent audits, including WebTrust audits by BDO International Limited, and the ministry is not involved in that audit. The impact on Indian websites and applications "has been very limited and for a very short period", the officials said.

CERT-In, India's computer emergency response team, published advisory CIAD-2026-0050 on October 21. It says the public disclosures it cites do not establish confirmed malicious use of the keys as of that date, and warns that removing emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from trust stores could leave legitimate certificates issued under that root untrusted and disrupt the sites that use them. It tells administrators to replace certificates that chain to the root where their clients will stop trusting it, and to confirm that their applications reject chains that pass through the compromised keys.

Red Hat published a security bulletin on October 21 that it rates Important. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 through 10 ship the affected hierarchy in their ca-certificates package, it says, and any product built on RHEL is potentially affected too, including containers built from RHEL and UBI images, RHEL CoreOS, OpenShift and OpenStack Platform. Updated packages had not been announced as of the bulletin's latest revision that day. Red Hat says the problem is not a software vulnerability in its products, and that an attacker would need one of the keys and a position to intercept a connection to exploit it.

Until the packages arrive, Red Hat's workaround for RHEL 7 and later blocks emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and the AAA Certificate Services root in the system trust store and rebuilds it, which also cuts off legitimate certificates under those roots unless they are added back by hand. RHEL 6 lacks the command the workaround uses, so those systems wait for the package. Customer containers should be rebuilt once the base images are updated, the bulletin says.

Canonical and Debian shipped updated ca-certificates packages on October 20, listed in the table above. Canonical notes that browsers on Ubuntu desktops are usually installed as snap packages that carry their own root store and update on their own schedule, so the package update does not cover them. Node.js released 26.12.1, 24.22.1 and 22.23.4 on October 21 with the key blocklist that was still a draft when this article was published, plus the NSS 3.131.1 root list.

(The story was updated after publication on October 21, to include the Indian government's investigation, the CERT-In and Red Hat advisories, and the Node.js, Ubuntu, Debian and Red Hat entries in the table of fixes.)

(Corrected on October 21: an earlier version said it was not known how the keys left eMudhra. The keys did not need to leave the company, because they were generated with so little randomness that anyone can compute them from the public certificates. The passages on the cause have been revised.)

Software Fixed in What it does Status

Go's filter sits in the standard library and rejects any chain containing one of the eight keys, on Go's own verifier and on the macOS and Windows system-verifier paths, and the change adds no setting to turn it off. A program picks it up only when rebuilt with the new release; Go 1.25 and older are out of support and get no fixes.

Several of the fixes work by removing roots rather than blocking the keys. certifi, webpki-roots, Homebrew's ca-certificates and the Debian and Ubuntu packages drop emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from their bundles. Debian and the Ubuntu releases older than 22.04 also drop Sectigo's AAA Certificate Services root, which Ubuntu 22.04 and later had already removed, and Homebrew drops that root and emSign Root TLS CA - G3 as well.

That also cuts off every legitimate certificate that chains to those roots. Mozilla, which made the same change to NSS, said some servers will become unavailable to non-Firefox users of its trust list until those servers move to new certificate chains. Canonical and Red Hat gave the same warning.

Jackson's site tracks a longer list, including the ca-certificates packages of Fedora, Arch, Alpine and Gentoo, curl's CA bundle, pip, uv and Electron, with FreeBSD and Bun still pending, and it warns that the curl built into macOS still accepts the chain because it checks against a bundle file that Apple has not updated.

Cloudflare, which learned of the problem on October 19, has released fixed WARP and 1.1.1.1 clients and cloudflared 2026.10.2, and said customers who run their own origin servers, mutual TLS or containers may need to update trust stores themselves.

Firefox needs nothing unless Remote Settings is disabled by policy or blocked on the network. The October 20 releases carry the block list for those installations.

None of the sources provide a way to detect past misuse of the keys beyond Chrome's CT search, which covers only logged certificates.

What Happens to eMudhra

Mozilla removed emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from NSS on October 20. Chrome will remove the same root in version 43 of its root store and is reviewing the status of eMudhra's other root in its store, emSign Root CA - G1, the Chrome Root Program said, citing the seriousness of the incident. The removal is expected to reach every device that relies on the Chrome Root Store on the morning of Tuesday, October 27, Pacific time, and earlier on Chrome Canary and Beta, Google said, so website operators with certificates chaining to that root must install a certificate from another hierarchy before then to avoid breakage. eMudhra has committed to moving those customers off the root, Google said.

Mozilla said it is working with the CA, other root programs and downstream trust stores on the root cause and will post more when it can. eMudhra's trust-services repository carried no notice about the incident as of October 20. The company posted a statement on its corporate site that day and issued a press release on October 21, covered in the first update below.

Go has not named the CA on its issue, where its release notes cite "specific security concerns around their operation", and a commenter asked for the hashes in the patch to be explained.

Filippo Valsorda, who maintains the cryptography packages in Go's standard library, replied that the keys are compromised and the certificates revoked, that Linux root stores are too poorly maintained for revocation to reach applications, and that putting the keys in code is the only option for now.

Roland Shoemaker of the Go security team later wrote on the issue that the team learned of the underlying problem on October 19 and kept the release notes deliberately vague, because the flaw was easy to exploit and the team expected it to become public that day. It became widely known only on October 20, he wrote.

Update: eMudhra Blames Flaw in April 2025 Key Ceremony

eMudhra Limited said in a press release filed with the BSE stock exchange on October 21 that the eight intermediates were created under its ECC root in a key generation ceremony on April 30, 2025, using hardware security modules certified to FIPS 140-2 Level 3, and that a flaw in that ceremony caused a key wrap and unwrap step, which packages a key for transfer and unpacks it again, to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys. The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores, the company said, and it is still working to establish the root cause.

The company said an independent researcher found over the weekend of October 17 that the weak keys could be reverse-engineered, "possibly with AI-assisted techniques", and reported this to Apple, Google, Microsoft and Mozilla.

Scott Helme, a security researcher, wrote that he recovered all eight private keys from the public certificates on his laptop in under a second, that one of them is the number 4 and the rest are also whole numbers below 256, and that an AI agent did the same from a single prompt.

eMudhra said its infrastructure was not compromised, no data was breached and its physical and logical security controls remained intact. It said the roots and issuing CAs had passed independent audits two years in a row and had been in browser trust lists since mid 2025, and that the incident has no connection with its Indian digital signature certificate and eSign businesses, which run on separate infrastructure.

The global TLS business accounts for around 1% of the company's revenue, it said, while acknowledging a reputational risk it cannot quantify. It is giving affected customers replacement certificates and is continuing its root-cause investigation with the root programs.

In the statement on its website, dated October 20, eMudhra said the incident does not affect its root CA private keys or its other intermediate CAs, that only one of the eight intermediates had been deployed in production, and that none of the eight, including that one, had issued any end-entity certificate.

eMudhra's shares fell 20% in Mumbai on October 21, Business Standard reported.

Update: India Opens Investigation as CERT-In and Red Hat Issue Advisories

India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has formed a special team to investigate the incident, senior ministry officials said on October 21, ThePrint reported. The officials said the ministry had taken serious note of the reported incident, is in contact with everyone involved to resolve it, and will share more once the investigation is complete.

The officials drew a line between eMudhra's two businesses. Its Indian digital signature certificate and eSign services are regulated by the Controller of Certifying Authorities under the ministry and are unaffected, they said. The certificates trusted by browsers and operating systems are an international business that runs under the global trust framework and is subject to independent audits, including WebTrust audits by BDO International Limited, and the ministry is not involved in that audit. The impact on Indian websites and applications "has been very limited and for a very short period", the officials said.

CERT-In, India's computer emergency response team, published advisory CIAD-2026-0050 on October 21. It says the public disclosures it cites do not establish confirmed malicious use of the keys as of that date, and warns that removing emSign ECC Root CA - G3 from trust stores could leave legitimate certificates issued under that root untrusted and disrupt the sites that use them. It tells administrators to replace certificates that chain to the root where their clients will stop trusting it, and to confirm that their applications reject chains that pass through the compromised keys.

Red Hat published a security bulletin on October 21 that it rates Important. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 6 through 10 ship the affected hierarchy in their ca-certificates package, it says, and any product built on RHEL is potentially affected too, including containers built from RHEL and UBI images, RHEL CoreOS, OpenShift and OpenStack Platform. Updated packages had not been announced as of the bulletin's latest revision that day. Red Hat says the problem is not a software vulnerability in its products, and that an attacker would need one of the keys and a position to intercept a connection to exploit it.

Until the packages arrive, Red Hat's workaround for RHEL 7 and later blocks emSign ECC Root CA - G3 and the AAA Certificate Services root in the system trust store and rebuilds it, which also cuts off legitimate certificates under those roots unless they are added back by hand. RHEL 6 lacks the command the workaround uses, so those systems wait for the package. Customer containers should be rebuilt once the base images are updated, the bulletin says.

Canonical and Debian shipped updated ca-certificates packages on October 20, listed in the table above. Canonical notes that browsers on Ubuntu desktops are usually installed as snap packages that carry their own root store and update on their own schedule, so the package update does not cover them. Node.js released 26.12.1, 24.22.1 and 22.23.4 on October 21 with the key blocklist that was still a draft when this article was published, plus the NSS 3.131.1 root list.

(The story was updated after publication on October 21, to include the Indian government's investigation, the CERT-In and Red Hat advisories, and the Node.js, Ubuntu, Debian and Red Hat entries in the table of fixes.)

(Corrected on October 21: an earlier version said it was not known how the keys left eMudhra. The keys did not need to leave the company, because they were generated with so little randomness that anyone can compute them from the public certificates. The passages on the cause have been revised.)

item.title: Hackers Hid Vasilek Backdoor in VMware Tools During 2-Year Russian Healthcare Intrusion (2026)
item.description:
A Belarus-aligned hacktivist group spent nearly two years within the network of a Russian healthcare organization.

According to a report published by Russian cybersecurity firm Solar, the activity has been attributed to a threat cluster dubbed Partisan Zmiy, which is also known as the Cyber Partisans.

Known to be active since at least 2020, the group has a track record of striking industrial enterprises and government agencies in Russia and Belarus with a backdoor called Vasilek that uses Telegram for command-and-control (C2) and data exfiltration.

Some of the attacks have also leveraged phishing lures to deliver an installer that simultaneously deploys the legitimate FortiClient VPN program on the system as well as an open-source program known as DNSCat2 that allows attackers to gain control of the infected host.

A notable aspect of the threat actor is their ability to stage destructive attacks with a wiper referred to as Pryanik, alongside taking steps to systematically clear Windows event logs using a utility dubbed Evlx.

The Rostelecom subsidiary said it discovered the intrusion in December 2025, although evidence suggests that the earliest signs of compromise date back to early 2024. The name of the targeted organization was not identified. The exact initial access vector used to breach the entity is also not known.

Unlike other attacks linked to Cyber Partisans, the threat actors remained on the network for an extended period of time without carrying out any destructive activity, marking something of a shift in modus operandi.

"The attacked organization possessed an extensive infrastructure and two-way trusted relationships with numerous subsidiary medical institutions," Solar said. "We hypothesize that the lack of infrastructure disruption is due precisely to the value of this access for further espionage and trusted relationship attacks."

Observed as part of the intrusion is a loader-scheduler service ("vmauad") that masquerades as a legitimate VMware component to maintain persistence and evade cursory inspection. To accomplish this, the attackers are said to have taken advantage of a trusted-but-unmonitored VMware Tools directory location to plant malicious executables or replace legitimate VMware DLLs with a malicious version ("vmtools.dll") containing the backdoor.

The primary responsibility of the Windows service is to launch the rogue binary "C:\Program Files\VMware\VMware Tools\authd.exe" that, besides launching a GOST tunnel every Saturday from 10 p.m. to 11 p.m., runs an updated version of Vasilek (version 1.5.8) once, eight hours after the service begins.

Once installed, Vasilek is equipped to collect information about an infected computer, execute Windows commands, launch and terminate processes, transfer files, capture screenshots, record keystrokes, and escalate privileges via runas. It can also prevent the machine from going into sleep mode, and update or remove itself.

One new addition is the "move_cursor" command that, as the name implies, allows the backdoor to move the cursor and simulate user input on the victim's screen.

"The group consistently invests in stealth and operational security, rather than new capabilities: hostname binding in two independent components, nightly scheduled payload launches, system proxy inheritance, disguise as legitimately installed but unused software, file rotation across the same paths, time-stomping, outgoing message suppression, and anonymous messages on behalf of the group in operator chats," Solar said.

"The backdoor's feature set has remained largely unchanged over four revisions. Due to Telegram being blocked in Russia by ISPs, communication between the Vasilek backdoor and C2 has become unstable."

The disclosure comes as Solar also disclosed details of a phishing campaign that employs JavaScript attachments mimicking business-themed documents, such as payments and purchase orders, to deliver a previously unreported malware family known as HypeAgent.

The Windows malware is a full-featured trojan designed to take complete control over infected systems, packing the ability to steal files, open a console, change desktop wallpaper, turn on a webcam, log keystrokes, launch hidden VNC and RDP sessions, control the mouse, and even deploy a cryptocurrency miner.

It's also capable of stealing cookies associated with Discord, Steam, GitHub, Instagram, Telegram, Binance, ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor, and tampering with the installed Exodus wallet app to inject JavaScript that can collect the victim's password, PIN, mnemonic phrase, and private key.

Earlier this June, Solar also observed legitimate infrastructure compromised by the ProxyCB proxyware botnet malware making automated requests to Russian websites and online platforms, while identifying possible overlaps between the botnet infrastructure and historical activity linked to TeamSpy, a threat cluster known for abusing TeamViewer to facilitate reconnaissance and data theft.

Last month, the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) charged Searzhudin Tamirlanovich Aktulaev, a 40-year-old Russian national extradited from Cyprus in May 2025, for exploiting an online messaging service of a well-known freelance employment platform to send malware-laced Excel attachments to about 80,000 of its users in 2016 and 2017 using 255 fake accounts.

The attacks led to the deployment of two types of malware, a variant of the TVRAT (aka Sheldor, SpyAgent, TeamBot, TeamSpy, and TVSPY) and DarkVNC, to harvest and send data from a victim computer to a remote server under the attacker's control. Thousands of computers are assessed to have been infected as a result of this scheme.

item.title: CISA Orders Federal Agencies to Patch Exploited Plex2Shell, Siemens, and SiteGuard Flaws (2026)
item.description:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added four vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, including four vulnerabilities impacting Plex Media Server that's collectively called Plex2Shell.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

  • CVE-2026-96652 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-96654 (CVSS score: 6.9) - Plex Media Server improper neutralization of encoded URI schemes in a web page Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-96655 (CVSS score: 5.3) - Plex Media Server Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-96656 (CVSS score: 8.6) - Plex Media Server external control of file name or path Vulnerability

According to security researcher Zach Main, who discovered and reported the vulnerabilities, a remote attacker could chain the four vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution. The issues were addressed in Plex Media Server 1.43.3.10861 released on August 3, 2026.

The addition of the four vulnerabilities to the KEV catalog follows a report from security researcher boredhackerblog, who found that threat actors are weaponizing the flaws to deploy cryptocurrency miners and proxy malware.

CISA has also flagged two other vulnerabilities as actively exploited. One of them is a DLL sideloading vulnerability in Siemens Software Center (CVE-2026-110936, CVSS score: 8.4) that has been abused in ClickFix attacks using a platform called Romulus.

The second security flaw is a command injection bug in EG Secure Solutions SiteGuard Server Edition (CVE-2026-106931, CVSS score: 8.5) that the Japanese company confirmed as being exploited. No additional details related to the exploitation activity are currently available.

CISA is urging Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply fixes for CVE-2026-106931, CVE-2026-96656, and CVE-2026-96654 by October 23, 2026, and the rest by November 3, 2026.

item.title: State Bank of India Confirms Data Leak After 3,897 Customer Records Found on Dark Web (2026)
item.description:
State Bank of India has identified 3,897 customer records containing personal information in a set of about 375,000 records available on the dark web, and it does not yet know where the data came from.

The state-owned bank, India's largest, said in a stock-exchange filing dated October 21 that it "has experienced an incident involving the loss of certain data." The count is preliminary, and the bank has yet to establish whether the data is authentic, how far the exposure goes and what risk it poses to customers.

The exposed information "reportedly included customers' registered mobile numbers, dates of birth, names, gender, email addresses, residential addresses, branch and CIF identifiers, lead IDs, and metadata associated with loan/lead records and other related files," in the filing's words. A CIF identifier is the customer information file number, the bank's internal ID for each customer.

The bank has not said whether the 3,897 records belong to 3,897 different people, or what the rest of the set contains. The 3,897 are roughly 1 in 100 of the records it examined.

Account numbers, balances, passwords, one-time passcodes, card details and government identity numbers such as PAN or Aadhaar are not among the categories the filing lists. The risk in the listed categories is impersonation: a caller or message that uses a customer's name, mobile number, date of birth, address, branch, and internal ID to appear to come from the bank.

The alert reached the bank on October 16 via its threat intelligence provider, CERT-In, India's national computer emergency response team, and the Defense Cyber Agency, the armed forces' cyber agency under the Ministry of Defense.

The bank activated its incident response and containment procedures and engaged an independent cybersecurity firm from CERT-In's panel of approved security auditors to assess what the filing calls "the alleged compromise."

The incident has no material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, the filing says. That covers the bank's business, not its customers.

The filing names no attacker, forum or dataset. The figure of about 375,000 matches a claim that the monitoring account CyberPulse56 flagged on X on October 16.

The account said a threat actor using the name Siriusim claimed to have leaked customer documents and personal data linked to SBI: 375,000 rows in CSV format and 2,722 PDF documents, said to include personal information, loan applications and supporting documents, account-opening forms and addresses.

The Free Press Journal examined the listing on BreachForums, a cybercrime forum used to trade stolen data, and found 4 sample records posted with the listing. The phone numbers in the samples were valid. The WhatsApp profile picture on one number matched the passport-size photograph on that person's KYC document, which the actor had also posted.

That check covers 4 records and does not show that the whole set is genuine or where it came from. The samples were mostly loan-related and carried KYC fields, and they did not show whether the data belonged to SBI itself, one of its subsidiaries, or a third-party provider that handles banking applications.

Nothing in the bank's filing ties its analysis to the listing, and the bank has not said whether the 2,722 PDF documents were part of what it examined.

Whether any SBI system was breached is an open question. The filing leaves the source of the data to the investigation and gives no date for when the data first appeared.

The filing does not mention whether affected customers have been or will be told. The bank's cyber security page, last updated in June, tells customers to report any cyber incident to report.phishing@sbi.co.in or the national cybercrime helpline, 1930. That is general advice, written before the incident.

Bank of Baroda, another state-owned bank, told the exchanges on July 27 about a cyber-security incident in nearly the same words, including "the alleged compromise," after receiving "a communication from an anonymous source claiming access to certain data." That filing named a preliminary cause, "potential business email compromise." SBI's names none.

item.title: U.S. Orders DeepSeek Removed From Federal Civilian Systems, Bans New Purchases (2026)
item.description:
U.S. federal civilian agencies must remove DeepSeek products from their information technology systems, along with any third-party products or services "developed using DeepSeek implementations," under a Department of Homeland Security order.

They may also no longer buy information technology products or services from the Chinese AI developer or its affiliates

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin issued the order, dated July 24, 2026, under the Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act of 2018, and the department published it in the Federal Register on October 20. The notice does not define "DeepSeek implementations."

The order names Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd., the developer of the R1 and V3 models, and covers its affiliates as defined in federal acquisition rules. The company's privacy policy says it collects, processes and stores users' personal data in the People's Republic of China.

Under the 2018 law, the Federal Acquisition Security Council recommends exclusion and removal orders, and three officials may issue them: the Secretary of Homeland Security for civilian agencies, the Secretary of Defense for the Defense Department and national security systems, and the Director of National Intelligence for the intelligence community.

The DeepSeek order therefore covers only what civilian agencies buy and run. It does not restrict companies or the public.

The 2018 law was first used in 2025, when the Director of National Intelligence excluded Acronis, a Swiss cybersecurity and data protection company, from intelligence community procurement and ordered its products removed from intelligence community systems.

Executive agencies "shall comply with exclusion and removal orders," the law says. An agency can ask the official who issued an order for an exception, and under the council's regulations the request must be in writing and give a compelling justification.

DHS directs questions about the order to CISA's FASCSA Order Implementation Team at fascsa.orders@cisa.dhs.gov.

The order also reaches government contractors. A federal contract that carries FAR clause 52.204-30 bars the contractor from providing or using, in performing the contract, any product or service covered by an applicable FASCSA order, unless the issuing official has granted a waiver.

The clause also requires the contractor to:

  • Search SAM.gov for the phrase "FASCSA order" at least once every three months
  • Make a reasonable inquiry into its supply chain when a new order could affect it
  • Report any covered product or service it has provided or used to the contracting officer within 3 business days of identifying it
  • Send further information on mitigation within 10 business days of that report
  • Include the clause in its subcontracts

An order issued after a solicitation applies to an existing contract only once the contracting officer adds it by amendment or modification.

The Federal Register notice gives no reasons for the order. The signed order is attached to the notice as four scanned pages and is posted on regulations.gov under docket DHS-2026-0628.

The order is dated July 24. DHS filed it for public inspection at the Federal Register on October 19, 87 days later, and it was published the next day.

The council's regulations leave public release of an order to the issuing official, who "May provide a copy of the order to other persons, including through public disclosure." They set no deadline for it.

The law requires the issuing official to notify the company named in an order and the appropriate congressional committees, and to review the order at least once a year.

Before the order, U.S. restrictions on DeepSeek were device bans adopted one body at a time. By February 2025, Congress, NASA, the Navy, the Pentagon and Texas had barred DeepSeek from government devices. Bills to bar DeepSeek on government devices were introduced in the House and Senate that month and had not advanced past committee as of October 21.

China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a briefing on October 20 that "China consistently opposes the overstretching of the concept of national security" and that Beijing will "resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese companies," the Associated Press reported. DeepSeek did not immediately respond to the AP's request for comment.

item.title: Attackers Abuse UpdraftCentral Keys to Plant Backdoors on WordPress Sites (2026)
item.description:
Unknown threat actors breached TeamUpdraft's website and potentially gained unauthorized access to customers' connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault, and UpdraftClone, using them to backdoor WordPress sites.

TeamUpdraft is the developer behind UpdraftPlus, a popular WordPress backup plugin with over four million active installations. The vendor also offers UpdraftCentral, a remote management service that's used for managing multiple sites remotely. A client component of UpdraftCentral is shipped within every copy of UpdraftPlus. 

"Over the weekend of 17-18 October we identified unauthorized access to the teamupdraft.com website," TeamUpdraft said in a statement. "Our team responded straight away and worked through the night to contain it – we closed the access route, signed out every account and replaced the keys and credentials that could have been affected."

As a result of the incident, threat actors are believed to have accessed its customer database, which holds the following information -

  • Names, email addresses, billing addresses and order history
  • Account passwords, stored only in hashed (scrambled) form and never in plain text
  • Two-factor authentication (2FA) settings
  • Connection keys for UpdraftCentral, UpdraftVault and UpdraftClone

TeamUpdraft said the database does not hold any financial information, and that they are handled by Stripe and PayPal. It also emphasized that the UpdraftPlus plugin, along with self-hosted versions of UpdraftCentral and backups sent to customers' own remote storage, are not impacted.

"However, if your site was accessed through UpdraftCentral, please also re-authorise your remote storage and change any storage access keys, as a precaution," it said.

In addition, TeamUpdraft said it deployed a fix to address the underlying issue, signed out every teamupdraft.com account and reset login security across the site, and released UpdraftPlus 1.26.13 (free) and 2.26.13 (Premium) to automatically disconnect every UpdraftCentral connection made before 10 p.m. BST on October 18, 2026, to prevent the old keys from working.

Other steps taken by the developer are listed below -

  • Disconnected every site from UpdraftVault and issued new credentials
  • Replaced every UpdraftClone client key
  • Rotated its keys with payment providers and other connected services
  • Implemented additional monitoring in place
  • Reported the incident to the U.K. Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) and other relevant authorities

Users who have a teamupdraft.com account are advised to change their password with immediate effect (and elsewhere, if the same password has been reused), reset 2FA settings, and exercise caution when receiving unexpected emails claiming to be from TeamUpdraft.

TeamUpdraft is also recommending that cloud customers of UpdraftCentral follow the steps below as soon as possible, since the connection keys can send commands to the connected sites -

  • Log in to the site's own WordPress dashboard, not through UpdraftCentral.
  • Update UpdraftPlus to version 1.26.12 (free) or 2.26.12 (Premium) or later.
  • Disconnect it from UpdraftCentral: go to Settings > UpdraftPlus > Advanced Tools > UpdraftCentral and delete the connection key.
  • Go to Users and check for any administrator accounts you don’t recognise. Remove them.
  • Go to Plugins, including the Must-Use tab if you can see it, and check for anything you don’t recognise. Remove it.
  • Change the passwords for all administrator accounts on the site.
  • If you find anything suspicious, consider restoring the site from a backup taken before 17 October.
  • Reconnect the site to UpdraftCentral.

UpdraftVault users are being urged to reconnect their sites to the backup service, and UpdraftClone users who have created a client key are required to copy the new keys from My Account > UpdraftClone > UpdraftClone Key Management and share them with their clients.

The development comes as WordPress security company Patchstack said it observed an attacker holding valid UpdraftCentral dashboard keys issuing commands to install backdoor plugins on connected WordPress sites. The campaign is said to have run continuously through an 18-hour window on October 18 and 19, 2026.

"The attacker sends a signed plugin.upload_plugin command over the plugin's remote procedure call channel, which listens on ordinary POST requests to the site root. WordPress installs and activates the supplied plugin through its standard installer," Patchstack security researcher Dave Jong said.

Slovakia-based penetration testing company Nethemba, which first detected the attack in the wild, has described the rogue plugin as a backdoor that hooks into every request to the site to check if the URL contains the parameter "?_9f5696=" and compares it with a 32-character token.

If a matching token is detected, it creates a user "data-ops43" with the display name "Site Tools," assigns it the Editor role, and grants the account "manage_options" and "install_plugins" permissions, allowing the operator to upload arbitrary PHP plugins and open site settings.

"Enabling registration and setting the default role to administrator is enough for the attacker to create a full administrator," Nethemba said. "On a standard WordPress site, an Editor also has unfiltered_html, so the account can put JavaScript into posts that runs in the browser of every administrator."

"The backdoor has a second layer as well. The account it creates, with a known password, stays in WordPress even after the plugin is removed, and the attacker can log in with it through the normal login form unless two-factor authentication is enabled for that account."

Although an early version of the plugin suffered from a coding error that causes impacted sites to fail with error 500, Nethemba said the threat actor deleted the broken backdoor by sending a "plugin.delete_plugin" command and then uploaded a working version that creates a full administrator account or logs in as an existing administrator.

WordPress site owners are advised to check for the following indicators of compromise -

  • Plugin names: Site Health Cache or Site Health 364F, Asset Forge 2, Content Helper, Wp Forge, Query Shelf, Style Bridge 8F5, Media Kit 183, Query Shelf, Post Dock 776, Nav Hub, Speed Desk, Speed Kit 300, Link Latch, Script Shelf, or Feed Case
  • Account names: system_team850, web.tech988, cmseditor170, cms.tech644 or web_mgr684, with an email at @example.com and a display name such as System Team, Web Tech, System Staff, System Ops, or Cms Tech
  • IP addresses: 43.250.53.42 and 2a09:bac5:4e21:2e3c::49b:9

In all, Patchstack said it observed 99 distinct backdoor plugin names, with each sample carrying the line "Small maintenance toolkit: keeps option storage tidy."

Wordfence, which published its own analysis of the incident, said a WordPress site may be affected if the below criteria are satisfied -

  • The site had UpdraftPlus Free or UpdraftPlus Premium installed and active while the affected UpdraftCentral connection key was present.
  • The site has, or had during the incident, an active connection key for TeamUpdraft’s cloud-hosted UpdraftCentral service.

"This is the second incident in this channel in five months," Patchstack warned. "In June 2026 the vendor fixed CVE-2026-10795 (CVSS 8.1), where an obsolete unsigned message format let an attacker forge UpdraftCentral commands with no keys at all. That was fixed in 1.26.5 and 2.26.5, but exploitation attempts continue, so sites below those versions face both problems at once."

The development comes days after the website of the Rank Math PRO WordPress plugin was hit by a software supply chain attack, causing users who downloaded version 3.0.123 between October 15 at 8:02 p.m. UTC and October 16 at 7:12 a.m. UTC to receive compromised versions that planted hidden backdoors.

The incident has been assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-111862 (CVSS score: 9.8). The issue was fixed in Rank Math PRO version 3.0.124.

"The malware may establish persistent access, communicate with rank1cdn[.]com, recreate hidden backdoors on page visits, and expose WordPress credentials, database credentials, API keys, and other secrets accessible to the web server," Wordefence said.

The findings also coincide with an advisory from PHP, which said it intends to ship a security release that fixes two critical vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, CVSS scores: 9.2), as information about the flaws leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. The flaws have been codenamed PHP2Shell.

According to watchTowr CEO Benjamin Harris, the vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8, and were originally due for release on October 22 at 11 a.m. ET. 

"PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," Huntress said. "When a critical bug lands in PHP itself, rather than in one app built on top of it, the number of places you have to go looking to identify vulnerable PHP versions gets very big, very fast."

Update

Patches have been released by the PHP Foundation for the two flaws, which can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code or expose sensitive process memory. In tandem, TeamUpdraft said it's taking its "support form temporarily offline" in light of the "ongoing issue affecting the PHP Foundation." Customers are advised to contact support via the support forums.
