item.title: China-Linked Hackers Use ARTEX AI Agents in ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack (2026)
item.description:
Microsoft on Wednesday disclosed that a China state-aligned actor dubbed Storm-0940 was behind the recent supply chain compromise of the ConnectWise Cloud Backup application.

During the incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX, a Go-based agentic AI penetration testing framework that was made closed-source in the wake of its abuse in cyber attacks targeting South Korean financial institutions, to speed up scanning and reconnaissance, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse at downstream victims.

The tech giant said the threat actor used the AI tool at "machine speed" to automate attacks targeting hundreds of organizations across the world spanning a broad range of sectors since September 2026. Targets include aerospace and defense, automotive, chemicals, energy, financial services, government, legal, manufacturing, media, military, semiconductor, software, technology, and think tanks and non-profits.

"Storm-0940's use of ARTEX accelerated the speed of compromised application abuse to authenticate to target environments through applications that had already been granted access, allowing the threat actor to operate without requiring an interactive user sign-in," Microsoft said.

"AI-accelerated follow-on activity included reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access."

Storm-0940 was first detailed by Microsoft in November 2024, revealing that the threat actor has been leveraging a botnet called Quad7 (aka CovertNetwork-1658) to conduct highly evasive password spray attacks. The threat actor is assessed to be active since at least 2021.

The adversary is also said to exploit internet-facing applications to gain initial access, followed by using compromised accounts to move through targeted environments. It has also been observed establishing persistence by adding credentials to existing OAuth applications within cloud infrastructures to ensure access to Microsoft 365 resources.

According to Microsoft, a chunk of these ARTEX-driven attacks have resulted in the adversary gaining privileged access to an organization's cloud infrastructure, including several instances where the time frame from initial targeting to privileged access was less than 3 hours.

In the case of the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 has been observed using ARTEX to attempt to sign in to more than 2,250 tenants at 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute, a pace the company said gives defenders a short window to detect and respond.

"Between October 10 and 14, 2026, Storm-0940 infrastructure at 144.172.64[.]99 conducted an automated cross-tenant password-spray campaign targeting 327 accounts across eight organizations to gain access to Microsoft 365 and Exchange Online," Microsoft said.

During this window, Microsoft said it captured over 151,000 failed logon events. The activity peaked on October 11 at 2,900 failures per minute, resulting in more than 111,000 failures in a single day. Of these, 48 accounts received more than 1,000 failures. No successful authentication, token issuance, Graph call, or directory change was detected, it noted.

That changed on October 15, 2026, when the AI agents gained access to the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications and began to use them to authenticate to customer environments.

"Additionally, after acquiring control of the identities of multiple ConnectWise cloud applications, the AI agents operating on behalf of the threat actor continued to use the same IP range to authenticate to customer environments using the illicit access acquired through these stolen app credentials, effectively taking advantage of the already established trust by these apps within a tenant," the tech giant added.

In some of these cases, the AI agents are assessed to have progressed beyond authentication to Microsoft Graph and directory operations. This included reconnaissance, application credential modifications to establish persistence, and changes involving identities, groups, and privileged roles.

The TAG-217 attack chain | Source: Zscaler

"The application credential modification made by Storm-0940’s associated agents in the targeted victims' environments can lead to persistence through other identities, credentials, and cloud services," Microsoft said. "These changes can remain active as a backdoor even after the original compromised application is mediated."

Storm-0940 is far from the only hacking crew to rely on ARTEX. Microsoft said it has observed threat actors across multiple geographic regions weaponizing the framework in their operations.

Recorded Future Insikt Group, which is tracking the threat cluster behind the attacks on South Korean financial institutions under the moniker TAG-217, said it identified activity linked to the hacking group dating back to August 17, 2026, when it "tested infrastructure designed to maintain remote access to computers and conducted internet scanning."

Over the next few weeks, the Chinese-speaking threat actor is said to have put together tools to attack cryptocurrency mining operations using the YiiMP platform, as well as set up a workspace for testing weaknesses in iPhones and modifying Android system software.

Zscaler ThreatLabz has since revealed that the attack's footprint extends beyond South Korea, and that it opportunistically targeted organizations around the globe and across multiple industry sectors. The findings come from a custom ARTEX deployment that included AI assistant configurations, synchronization scripts, network routing tools, and a Claude Code prompt history.

"ARTEX was configured to use a DeepSeek model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, but other configurations also specified DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok," security researcher Seongsu Park said. "Prompts directed AI models to divide investigation tasks and review one another's findings, including instructions for GLM to review work performed by DeepSeek and its subagents."

An analysis of the prompt histories has revealed requests for bulk personal and transaction data, along with questions about selling stolen data, suggesting the attacks were likely financially motivated. Other prompts related to extracting payment gateway API keys, exploiting NFT minting workflows, and gaining unauthorized administrative privileges.

The findings once again highlight how threat actors are increasingly integrating agentic AI tools into their offensive security workflows to quickly carry out attacks at scale.

"Agents are not constrained by factors affecting humans – they can work around the clock, on weekends, and on holidays and attempt multiple breach paths simultaneously, enabling significantly reduced time from selecting a target to achieving objectives, increasing the speed and impact of complex attacks like supply chain compromises," Microsoft said.

In response to the findings, ConnectWise said the activity "describes a campaign that reaches well beyond any one company," adding "nation-state actors are increasingly targeting the software supply chain, because one trusted connection can open the door to many organizations."

"AI now lets them test those connections at [...] 'machine speed.' MSPs are in the middle of that chain. They are targets in their own right, and they are also a path into every client they serve. Every vendor and every MSP must defend itself with both of those risks in mind."

ConnectWise, which temporarily shut down services following the attacks, has been restoring services in phases, a process that it said will take several days.

item.title: Someone Tried to Exploit PHP2Shell 4 Days Before the Vulnerabilities Were Publicly Disclosed (2026)
item.description:
Amazon's Threat Intelligence team on Wednesday said it detected an attempt to exploit the newly disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities on October 17, 2026, against its MadPot honeypot service, as the flaws come under broad exploitation in the wild following the release of the patches.

"The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network," CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said in a post shared with The Hacker News.

"While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure."

The attempt, Amazon said, was recorded from "103.216.220[.]92," an IP address geolocated to Australia.

The activity relates to a set of two vulnerabilities impacting PHP core, both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scoring system. Tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and discovered by researchers from Calif, OpenAI, and Google-owned Wiz, the flaws can be abused to achieve pre-authentication remote code execution on affected systems.

The shortcomings are present in every PHP release from the 7.x and 8.x series, and pose a risk to every reachable PHP endpoint on an affected server, including static forms, login routes, and health checks. According to CrowdStrike, an attack exploiting the flaws leaves virtually no digital traces.

"There is no authentication to bypass, no session to steal, and no vulnerable endpoint to discover," CrowdStrike said. "The exposure is independent of the CMS, framework, or plug-ins in use."

"Worker processes remain stable, responses return HTTP 200, and application logs record no anomalies, because no application code ever ran. The only server-side trace is a single memory-limit fatal in the web server's error log, which is routinely dismissed as noise, leaving defenders without actionable web telemetry to identify compromised endpoints."

Originally scheduled for coordinated disclosure on October 22, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. UTC, details about the CVE identifiers and a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit leaked ahead of time, prompting the PHP Foundation to move the release forward by one day.

"Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling," the PHP Foundation said. "Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions."

Amazon said it detected multiple PoC exploits for PHP2Shell coinciding with the day of the release of the fixes, with the earliest attempt flagged around October 21, 2026, at 2 a.m. UTC.

This was followed by additional exploitation attempts from anonymized infrastructure over the next six hours. The variety of payloads and the anonymization infrastructure used indicate that multiple threat actors are involved, Amazon Threat Intelligence said.

The attempts have been recorded from the following IP addresses on October 21, 2026 -

  • 31.223.184[.]166
  • 37.19.200[.]5
  • 134.209.159[.]64
  • 103.114.163[.]188
  • 95.217.98[.]37

According to ELLIO, the first PHP2Shell request targeting its sensors was observed on October 21, 2026, at 8:36 a.m. UTC, less than an hour after "Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix."

"Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed," the PHP Foundation said. "Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure."

The severity of the vulnerabilities has prompted warnings from international cybersecurity agencies such as the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), urging organizations to apply the fixes as soon as possible or consider taking them offline.

"Monitor web servers for suspicious activity, including PHP processes unexpectedly launching command shells or downloading files," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an X post. "Ensure appropriate process-monitoring capabilities are in place to help identify potential exploitation."

In a similar alert, the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) said the vulnerabilities can provide threat actors with a direct path to the server's file system or database. OpenAI, which described the flaws as "one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory," has released a Codex skill to check if a website or local PHP binary is vulnerable to PHP2Shell.

With PHP powering a majority of the websites in the world, the vast attack surface, coupled with the severity and ease of exploitation of the PHP2Shell flaws, poses major risks as it allows unauthenticated attackers to execute code and steal sensitive data.

"PHP is used by almost 70% of websites," Cloudflare said. "The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the internet."

VulnCheck's analysis has identified PHP on 2,608,039 internet-facing hosts, out of which over 700,000 hosts run PHP 3.x through 7.3. Another set of about 400,000 hosts run PHP versions 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1, while 403,000 hosts run supported 8.2 through 8.5 branches.

In a similar breakdown, Modat said it detected 4.38 million internet-facing PHP services as of October 20, 2026, with 79% (i.e., about 3.47 million) of them on a branch that PHP no longer supports (4.x, 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1). PHP 7.4, which reached end-of-life in 2022, accounts for 878,761 services, followed by PHP 5.3 with 486,684 services and PHP 7.2 with 461,965 services.

"PHP is a massively popular language, and powers large parts of the internet," Ilkka Turunen, Field CTO at Sonatype, said in a statement. "The immediate priority is clear accountability: know where PHP is used across your services and products, who owns remediation, and how quickly fixes can be deployed."

"It is likely there is a long tail of environments needing to apply this patch as PHP is bundled into many other operating system distributions, as well as is found in many historic environments."

Some of the other notable developments are listed below -

  • WebOps platform has blocked over 60,000 suspicious requests probing the vulnerability as of October 21, 2026, at 7:08 p.m. PDT.
  • VulnCheck has identified two hosts, 85.11.167[.]243 and 45.198.224[.]169, with the user-agent "php2shell-scan/109618" weaponizing CVE-2026-109618 to target its honeypots, while 109.71.252[.]97 has leveraged both the flaws.
  • Cloudflare has observed attack traffic targeting its customers, with threat actors "mutating the attack payload to try to bypass our protections by tracking the volume of matches and cross-referencing with the rule logic."
  • CloudLinux has released fixed packages for ea-php52 through ea-php85 and every alt-php version.
  • JFrog has observed fake PoC exploits and prank malware being published on GitHub that change the victim's wallpaper to NSFW content.
  • Additional guidance and mitigations have been published by numerous security and software vendors, including Akamai, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Arctic Wolf, Automattic, Cisco Talos, Coalition, Corelight, CyCognito, Datadog, Debian, Endor Labs, Expel, Fastly, Fortinet, Google Cloud, Hadrian, Huntress, Imperva, Intruder, Kaspersky, Microsoft Azure, NetSPI, Orca Security, OX Security, Palo Alto Networks Unit 42, Patchstack, Pentest Tools, Qualys, Rapid7, Recorded Future, ReliaQuest, Sansec, SOCRadar, Searchlight Cyber, SolarWinds, Sophos, Tanium, Tenable, Trend Micro, Ubuntu, Vercel, watchTowr, Wordfence, and Zscaler.
  • Government agencies across the world have also issued advisories for the vulnerabilities: the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD), the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (CCCS), CERT-EU, CISA, Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA), the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA), the Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), U.K.'s NCSC, NCSC-NL, and NSA. 

"The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons," Moses said. "In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them.."

"That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed."

Amazon's Threat Intelligence team on Wednesday said it detected an attempt to exploit the newly disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities on October 17, 2026, against its MadPot honeypot service, as the flaws come under broad exploitation in the wild following the release of the patches.

"The exploit attempt originated from an IP address associated with a commercial anonymization network," CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, said in a post shared with The Hacker News.

"While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure."

The attempt, Amazon said, was recorded from "103.216.220[.]92," an IP address geolocated to Australia.

The activity relates to a set of two vulnerabilities impacting PHP core, both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scoring system. Tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and discovered by researchers from Calif, OpenAI, and Google-owned Wiz, the flaws can be abused to achieve pre-authentication remote code execution on affected systems.

The shortcomings are present in every PHP release from the 7.x and 8.x series, and pose a risk to every reachable PHP endpoint on an affected server, including static forms, login routes, and health checks. According to CrowdStrike, an attack exploiting the flaws leaves virtually no digital traces.

"There is no authentication to bypass, no session to steal, and no vulnerable endpoint to discover," CrowdStrike said. "The exposure is independent of the CMS, framework, or plug-ins in use."

"Worker processes remain stable, responses return HTTP 200, and application logs record no anomalies, because no application code ever ran. The only server-side trace is a single memory-limit fatal in the web server's error log, which is routinely dismissed as noise, leaving defenders without actionable web telemetry to identify compromised endpoints."

Originally scheduled for coordinated disclosure on October 22, 2026, at 2:00 p.m. UTC, details about the CVE identifiers and a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit leaked ahead of time, prompting the PHP Foundation to move the release forward by one day.

"Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling," the PHP Foundation said. "Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions."

Amazon said it detected multiple PoC exploits for PHP2Shell coinciding with the day of the release of the fixes, with the earliest attempt flagged around October 21, 2026, at 2 a.m. UTC.

This was followed by additional exploitation attempts from anonymized infrastructure over the next six hours. The variety of payloads and the anonymization infrastructure used indicate that multiple threat actors are involved, Amazon Threat Intelligence said.

The attempts have been recorded from the following IP addresses on October 21, 2026 -

  • 31.223.184[.]166
  • 37.19.200[.]5
  • 134.209.159[.]64
  • 103.114.163[.]188
  • 95.217.98[.]37

"Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed," the PHP Foundation said. "Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure."

"Monitor web servers for suspicious activity, including PHP processes unexpectedly launching command shells or downloading files," the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said in an X post. "Ensure appropriate process-monitoring capabilities are in place to help identify potential exploitation."

In a similar alert, the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) said the vulnerabilities can provide threat actors with a direct path to the server's file system or database. "The php2shell vulnerabilities affect the PHP runtime itself and can allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers, expose customer data, or disrupt services. Because PHP underpins widely used platforms such as WordPress and Magento, these flaws could potentially affect a large number of applications across the internet."

item.title: New QPACK Flaws Can Crash HTTP/3 Servers, Trigger Up to 4,000-Fold Memory Amplification (2026)
item.description:
A remote attacker who has not logged in can crash many HTTP/3 web servers with a single connection, security firm FoxIO disclosed, releasing working proof-of-concept code.

By sending a small batch of compressed HTTP headers that expands in memory to a much larger set, the attacker can force the server to use thousands of times more memory than it received, enough to run a default server out of memory.

The flaws cause only denial-of-service attacks, with no evidence of data theft or code execution and no public reports of attacks in the wild. Fixes are out for quic-go, Cloudflare quiche, lsquic and Wireshark, but Bun, the h3 Rust library and aioquic were still unpatched at disclosure.

FoxIO found the same class of flaw in seven of ten HTTP/3 stacks it tested. The common cause is in QPACK, the scheme HTTP/3 uses to compress request headers so repeated fields travel as a short code instead of the full text.

A server is supposed to cap the size of the headers after it unpacks them. The affected stacks cap the compressed batch that arrives on the wire, but not the unpacked result, or they apply the cap too late, so a single request can expand into hundreds of thousands of header entries that the server holds in memory.

The reach is wide because these stacks sit under common software. quic-go is the Go library behind Caddy, Traefik and cloudflared; lsquic is LiteSpeed's library, used in LiteSpeed Web Server and OpenLiteSpeed; and Bun's HTTP/3 server runs on lsquic.

The attacker needs no account or special access, and since HTTP/3 runs over UDP, the request reaches the server before much of the usual filtering applies.

Which stacks are fixed and which are still exposed, as of October 22, 2026:

Stack Status Fixed version Identifier
quic-go Fixed 0.57.0 CVE-2025-64702
Cloudflare quiche Fixed 0.29.3 CVE-2026-12523
lsquic Fixed 4.9.0 no CVE
Wireshark Fixed 4.6.2 / 4.4.12 CVE-2025-13945
Bun Unpatched — no CVE
h3 (hyperium) Unpatched — no CVE
aioquic / mitmproxy Unpatched — no CVE

FoxIO lists IIS, Envoy, ngtcp2/nghttp3, and Google's quiche as not affected, each because it caps the unpacked headers while decoding rather than after.

The amplification varies by stack, in FoxIO's own tests against default settings. On quic-go, a 1 MB compressed batch unpacked into about 160,000 header fields and left roughly 15 MB held in the request, about 17 times the bytes sent; quic-go's own advisory puts the possible expansion at around 50 times.

A second method drives the ratio much higher: the attacker stores one roughly 4 KB header entry, then points at it thousands of times using one-byte references, and the server rebuilds the full entry on each reference. FoxIO measured about 4,000 times on Bun and between 600 and 1,800 times on lsquic.

Bun carries a worst-case. Its HTTP/3 server, which Bun's documentation calls experimental, uses lsquic but replaces the part that caps header memory with its own code, which checks each header but never the running total. FoxIO found that once the unpacked headers pass 2 GB, a size counter in that code overflows to zero and the server enters a loop it never leaves.

A single stream carrying about 516 KB on the wire, FoxIO reported, leaves the server stuck at 100 percent CPU with no recovery, blocking new requests. The missing running total is what lets the overflow be reached; lsquic's own 64 KB cap prevents it.

Wireshark is a different case from the server flaws. Its issue crashes the HTTP/3 dissector, the part that reads HTTP/3 out of a capture, when Wireshark decrypts traffic using a key-log file or opens a capture file that holds decryption secrets. It is not a server an attacker reaches over the network. Wireshark said it is "unaware of any exploits for this issue."

Operators should upgrade to the fixed releases above. For the stacks with no fix, FoxIO gives interim steps: on Bun, do not expose an HTTP/3 server; on mitmproxy, turn off HTTP/3 by passing --set http3=false; and for the h3 Rust library, set a sensible limit with max_field_section_size.

The lsquic fix, released July 16, 2026, caps how many unpacked header sets a server holds per stream, defaulting to one. FoxIO said the work began after Gal Bar Nahum's research into "MadeYouReset," a denial-of-service technique against HTTP/2, which asked whether HTTP/3's header compression had a similar weakness.

item.title: Node.js Brotli Decoder Bug Could Allow Remote Code Execution in All Supported Versions (2026)
item.description:
Node.js released security updates on October 21 for its three supported release lines, 22.x, 24.x and 26.x, fixing 10 flaws. The most serious is a bug in the Brotli decompression code that Node.js bundles, which the project says can allow remote code execution, meaning an attacker could run code of their choosing on the affected system.

Each supported line has one fixed version: 22.23.4 and 24.22.1 on the long-term support lines, and 26.12.1 on the current line. Node.js 20.x and earlier have reached end of life and will not receive the fix, so they should be moved to a supported line.

The Brotli flaw is in code Node.js bundles, not in a user's own program. Node.js runs that code whenever it decompresses Brotli data, either directly through the node:zlib module or automatically when code calls fetch() on a response sent with Brotli compression.

An application is exposed where it decompresses Brotli data an attacker controls, such as a request body or a response fetched from another server.

The Brotli Flaw

The flaw is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder, set off by malformed compressed input. The fix is an upstream patch from the Brotli project that Node.js copied in, and it makes the decoder catch invalid input and stop earlier rather than writing past the buffer.

Brotli is Google's compression library, and Node.js ships its own copy. The same fix shipped in Brotli 1.2.1, 1.1.1, and 1.0.10 on October 21, so other software that bundles Brotli may need the same update. The change was first made in Brotli's source in February 2026 and shipped as a security release only in October.

"Remote code execution" is the project's description of what the flaw could allow, and the flaw is rated high rather than critical. How far that has been shown in practice is narrower.

A public proof-of-concept published on October 22 reached code execution only against a deliberately weakened test build. On a standard Node.js build, its author reported a crash and a limited read of process memory, not code execution, and said a working attack on a normal build was not achieved.

Patched Node.js rejects the malformed input the proof-of-concept uses, and no exploitation of the flaw in the wild has been reported as of October 22.

The Other Flaws

Three of the other fixes are also rated high. Two are TLS certificate checks an attacker could bypass by writing a server's IP address in an unusual form, so a certificate matches a host it should not (CVE-2026-106069 and CVE-2026-105483). The third stops dns.resolve from cutting a hostname short at an embedded null byte (CVE-2026-105482).

Node.js rates CVE-2026-105483 high, though the commit that fixed it calls the bug low-severity and hard to exploit.

The rest are medium and low severity. One medium flaw makes crypto.randomUUID() and crypto.randomInt() hand back the same values in every process when an application is built as a startup snapshot or a single-executable application (CVE-2026-106074), which undermines anything that relies on those values being unpredictable.

The full set, and the lines each one affects:

CVE What it is Severity Affected lines
CVE-2026-111497 Out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder; remote code execution, per the project High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x
CVE-2026-106069 TLS hostname-check bypass when a host resolves to an IP address in non-canonical form High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x
CVE-2026-105483 TLS hostname-check bypass when an IP is written in fullwidth digits High 24.x, 26.x
CVE-2026-105482 dns.resolve truncates names that contain a null byte High 22.x, 24.x, 26.x
CVE-2026-105481 Keep-alive socket can process a response written before the request was sent Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x
CVE-2026-106072 Certificate validation for non-canonical IPv4 lets DNS names authenticate IP endpoints Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x
CVE-2026-106074 randomUUID() and randomInt() caches reused in startup snapshots and single-executable apps Medium 22.x, 24.x, 26.x
CVE-2026-106070 ZipFile returns attacker-controlled bytes after a failed header check Low 26.x
CVE-2026-106071 Permission Model over-grants file access through a wildcard lookup Low 26.x
CVE-2026-106073 Permission Model bypass with fs.realpathSync Low 22.x, 24.x, 26.x

The eMudhra Certificate Block

The same updates also stop Node.js from trusting eight intermediate certificate authority keys from the Indian provider eMudhra that were reported compromised days earlier.

Node.js uses the Mozilla root certificate list but does not perform revocation checks by default, so before this update, a certificate chain built on one of the compromised keys still passed.

The releases add a built-in block on the eight keys and update the bundled root list to remove three emSign roots. Go made the same block in its own update on October 20.

Connections resumed from a session that began before the update are not re-checked until that session times out, and end-of-life lines do not get the block.

Updated Dependencies

Beyond the 10 flaws, the updates refresh several bundled parts. The copy of undici, the HTTP client behind fetch(), moves to a version that fixes three moderate advisories: one in its Subresource Integrity check and two memory-exhaustion flaws, one of them in the WebSocket client built into Node.js.

Node.js also updated its bundled c-ares on all lines, OpenSSL on 22.x and 24.x, and SQLite on 22.x, to include fixes for publicly known vulnerabilities.

If You Cannot Upgrade Yet

Upgrading is the fix. The advisory offers no temporary workaround for the Brotli flaw, so an application that cannot upgrade immediately has no fallback within Node.js itself.

Vercel, which runs Node.js for its customers, said it added firewall rules on October 21 that block the attack in inbound requests. The rules do not cover Brotli responses an application fetches from other servers, and do not replace upgrading.

item.title: LiteLLM Suspects GitHub Token Leak in AI Gateway Logs Behind Malicious Package Release (2026)
item.description:
LiteLLM on Wednesday disclosed that threat actors compromised "multiple independent security controls" to push a malicious version of the Python package containing a credential stealer and a backdoor.

On October 21, 2026, LiteLLM's release pipeline was compromised to push 1.107.0 to the Docker Hub registry and the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. The incident took place around 4:00 a.m. PST. The following compromised versions were published -

  • LiteLLM v1.107.0 (PyPI)
  • v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable (Docker)
  • v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable (GHCR)

Users who downloaded an unpinned version of LiteLLM between 11:39 a.m. and 1:23 p.m. UTC via pip or used the Docker image v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, or main-stable between 11:46 a.m. and 2:20 p.m. UTC are impacted.

The poisoned version incorporated code to harvest credentials and keys, and run arbitrary code from a remote server every hour, turning it into a remote access trojan (RAT).

Specifically, the Python interpreter processes a path file ("cook.pth"), which includes a command to import "cook," a Python script ("cook.py") that deobfuscates itself and runs a stealer routine named "privcollect" to gather system, browser, developer, cloud, and AI tool secrets, and exfiltrate the data to "litellm[.]dev/healthcheck" via an HTTP POST request.

In addition, the interpreter attempts to execute "sitecustomize.py," which runs only on Linux and macOS machines, and is configured to fetch "domain.txt" from a now-removed GitHub dead drop ("github[.]com/letters9813"). Should this file return a valid response, the malware proceeds to download a second-stage Python script from "<domain>/codepy" and execute it.

item.title: OpenCode Flaw Lets Malicious MCP Servers Execute Code During Sign-In on Windows and WSL (2026)
item.description:
A flaw in the OpenCode AI coding agent allowed a malicious or hijacked MCP server to run code on a developer's Windows or WSL machine when the developer signed in. OpenCode connects to MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers to add outside tools, and such code would run with the developer's own access.

Anomaly, the company behind OpenCode, fixed the flaw in version 1.18.33 on September 28. It did not request a CVE or publish a security advisory, so vulnerability scanners will not flag the builds still at risk: 1.0.137 through 1.18.32.

During that sign-in, the server itself supplies the web address the user is sent to, an OAuth "authorization endpoint." On Windows and WSL, OpenCode handed that address to a helper that opens it in a browser. The helper built a PowerShell command around the address without escaping it, so an address written to carry a PowerShell command would run that command.

The browser step runs only when a developer starts the sign-in, by running opencode mcp auth or making the matching request. Having the server configured, or opening a session, does not reach it.

The attacker needs control of a remote MCP server the developer has added, and that server need not be hostile from the start. One that is later taken over, or a domain that changes hands, could carry the same address.

Pillar Security, which found the flaw and disclosed it on October 19, rates it critical, with a proposed severity score of 9.8 out of 10.

The flaw affects OpenCode on Windows and the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). macOS and Linux are not affected, because OpenCode opens the browser there without passing the address through a shell.

OpenCode shipped the fix as a routine change. The pull request that carried it is described as a refactor of browser-launch code, and neither it nor the release notes mention a security flaw.

Anomaly did not request a CVE or publish an advisory. Its security policy says MCP servers that a user configures are "outside our trust boundary."

Pillar reported the flaw privately on August 29 and later asked Anomaly to reconsider and request a CVE. Anomaly's answer was that a malicious MCP server falls outside its threat model, according to Pillar.

Because there is no CVE, the flaw will not show up in scanners or dependency alerts, so finding affected installs means checking the OpenCode version directly. Anomaly has published advisories for other OpenCode code-execution flaws this year, including one fixed in August.

The same kind of flaw has surfaced before. In July 2025, the mcp-remote proxy carried an almost identical bug, in which a malicious server's authorization endpoint reached the command line. It was assigned CVE-2025-6514.

OpenCode's browser helper is a widely used package called open. Its Windows behavior was reported as a command-injection risk in 2023 and fixed in open's version 11, but OpenCode stayed on an older release.

The usual defense for this class is to check that the address uses HTTP or HTTPS. It does not help here, because the attack uses an ordinary HTTPS address. OpenCode added that check as well, but the hole was closed by updating it to the fixed version.

What to Do

Anyone running OpenCode on Windows or WSL should upgrade and check which servers they are connected to.

  1. Upgrade to OpenCode 1.18.33 or later.
  2. If you cannot upgrade yet, remove any remote MCP servers you have not vetted from your OpenCode configuration.
  3. Run opencode mcp list to see which servers are configured.

Pillar reported no signs that the flaw has been used in attacks and published no indicators to check for past exploitation. The flaw is separate from a breach of OpenCode's hosted Console disclosed around the same time, which may have exposed some users' stored API keys for OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

item.title: Railway Says Intruder May Have Accessed Customer Secrets, Urges Credential Rotation (2026)
item.description:
Platform-as-a-Service (PaaS) provider Railway on Wednesday disclosed "anomalous activity" related to systems that store customer environment variables.

Upon further investigation, the company found that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to encrypted environment variables, and, in some cases, obtained the decrypted contents. The impact, it said, is limited to a "subset of users," although it did not disclose an exact number.

Environment variables refer to user-defined key-value pairs that are used to store sensitive data like API keys, database credentials, or feature flags. They are configured at the operating system or container environment level instead of hard-coding the values directly into a program's source code.

Railway said the incident is likely part of a series of attacks designed to target platform companies with the ultimate goal of compromising artificial intelligence (AI) inference providers. The company also said it has notified upstream providers to proactively revoke the keys so as to prevent their abuse.

Customers are being urged to take the following actions as a precautionary measure -

  • Rotate environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as private registry credentials.
  • Review logs for those services for unusual activity

According to security researcher Taylor Monahan (@tayvano_), the incident has also allowed the attackers (0xd9773325282874d18cb83f1fe50f14c39750b2ee) to drain cryptocurrency wallets whose private keys were stored on Railway. The first known cryptocurrency theft transaction is said to have occurred at 7:36 p.m., at least two hours before the incident was officially disclosed. 

Railway has since rotated all Railway bucket credentials and invalidated Railway API tokens in response to the incident. It has also restored builds for Pro and Enterprise workspaces, allowing customers to apply new credentials added in Railway.

"Builds remain available for Pro and Enterprise workspaces," it said. "We are continuing to work on enabling builds for Hobby, then Free and Trial. Some builds are still failing more often than usual, and many deployments remain queued with longer than usual wait times. We are continuing to work on both."

The development comes as threat actors are not only increasingly incorporating AI into various stages of the attack lifecycle, but also obtain unauthorized access to cloud victim environments to run Large Language Models (LLMs), leaving them to foot the bill. This approach is called LLMjacking.

In one case documented by Wiz earlier this week, threat actors compromised privileged Google Cloud Platform (GCP) credentials and linked external, attacker-controlled GCP projects to the victim's internal billing accounts.

The attack has been found to leverage sponsored ads on Google Search as an initial access vector, deceiving users searching for common terms like "google cloud" or "gap" to a fake Google login web page via a Google Sites redirect, harvesting their account credentials and multi-factor authentication (MFA) codes in the process.

Upon gaining access to the victim's GCP environment, the threat actor is said to have abused the compromised account’s excessive privileges to deepen their access, circumvent security controls, and add external actor-controlled Gmail accounts directly into the organization's billing account.

"Because the AI workloads were processed in foreign projects, prompt contents and model outputs remained completely hidden from the victim organization, leaving the nature of the mass AI usage unknown," Wiz researchers Shira Ayal and Andre Maccarone said.

These resource abuse cases are not isolated. According to the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, attackers are targeting exposed LLM endpoints to power an autonomous cybercrime operation capable of scanning the internet, exploiting vulnerabilities, stealing credentials, and mining cryptocurrency without human intervention for up to 100,000 steps.

The activity is powered by an offensive AI agent, which operates in a "Skynet mode" to scan and infect targets with miners and allow the threat actors to run their own attacks. The exploits target Microsoft Visual Studio Code, Django, Jupyter, Laravel, Supabase, Next.js, and Flask/Werkzeug deployments.

The end goal is free inference. Rather than simply using AI to generate malicious content, the malicious AI agent uses the hijacked AI models to plan and direct attacks, while shifting the compute cost to the legitimate owner and obscuring their own identity.

Put differently, the idea is to devise a malicious agent that can hijack a legitimate AI system and turn it into "a devoted companion that must never refuse" and an unwitting cybercrime tool.

"The captured instructions defined a single agent equipped for internet-wide scanning, exploitation of several common web frameworks, database theft, credential and secret harvesting, and cryptocurrency mining," the Symantec Threat Hunter Team said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

"The activity is a form of LLMjacking, where attackers steal access to someone else's AI model so that the victim pays for the computing power."

item.title: The AI Agent Nobody Owns: Watch Expert Webinar On Your Newest Insider Threat (2026)
item.description:
Right now, there is probably an AI agent running on a laptop somewhere in your network. It stores API keys and database passwords, can access your internal systems, and works without anyone watching.

Nobody reviewed its access. Nobody owns it.

If an employee had that much reach with that little oversight, you would call it an insider risk. So why do we still call the agent a productivity tool?

Most of the conversation about AI security is about what threat actors are doing with it. But the bigger threat may already be inside your organization.

That's the focus of our upcoming webinar, AI as an Insider Threat: From Shadow AI to Governed AI, with expert guest Richard De La Torre, Technical Product Marketing Manager at Bitdefender. Save your seat for a practical security playbook on bringing that unseen AI under control.

Where AI is hiding on your endpoints

It isn't only developers. AI agents, coding assistants, MCP servers, and browser extensions are turning up across the business.

And most of them never cross your network gateway in a way the tools you already run would recognize.

The result is a hard irony. The AI with the most access is often the AI your security team can't see.

📅 Save Your Spot: Watch the Webinar

The visibility gap, by the numbers

According to Bitdefender's 2026 Cybersecurity Assessment report, only 51.8% of organizations report having full visibility into the AI tools their staff use. That leaves nearly half without the full picture.

That blind spot has a cost. IBM found that 20% of breached organizations were compromised through shadow AI.

Which raises the question: what can organizations realistically do about it? That's exactly what the webinar gets practical about. Register now to see what a lean team can do about the AI it can't yet see.

From shadow AI to governed AI

New research from Bitdefender Labs looks at what's really running on endpoints, based on real machines; among the findings: a malicious agent skill caught in the wild.

Blocking AI outright is the obvious response, but it tends to fail. The alternative is governed adoption, and the session shows what that looks like in practice.

What you'll take away

  • Where AI is actually showing up on your endpoints, and why the tools you already run don't see most of it.
  • New research from Bitdefender Labs on real machines, including the malicious agent skill caught in the wild.
  • Why an AI agent with credentials and no owner behaves like an insider risk, and what to do about it.
  • Why blocking AI outright tends to fail, and what governed adoption looks like instead.

The AI already running on your endpoints won't wait for a policy. Join expert guest Richard De La Torre, Technical Product Marketing Manager at Bitdefender, and save your seat for AI as an Insider Threat.
